channel.description: 语言与大脑、结构与功能、脑疾病机理、静息态与自然刺激的文献观察

item.title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
For two decades, most tractography has mapped brain connections by sampling millions of pathways probabilistically. Sampling makes results non-deterministic and costly to store. We show that it is unnecessary: modeling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain gives the expected result of infinitely many streamlines. This approach is more reliable than streamline-based tractography across test--retest scans. It readily maps tracts in clinical-grade data and neonates, around tumors and along small pathways. MPAT is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rokemlab/mpat .

item.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

item.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. Here, we evaluated whether repeated at-home recordings using a four-channel consumer EEG device could provide meaningful electrophysiological measurements and characterized the stability of these measures across sessions. Five participants completed repeated recordings across multiple days, including resting-state measurements and an auditory oddball task performed with and without concurrent cognitive load. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. Measurement stability varied across electrophysiological features, and aggregating repeated sessions improved the consistency of individual-level estimates. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

item.title: Bivariate Multiscale Sample Entropy of Frontoparietal-Subgenual ACC Dynamics in Depression During Accelerated TMS at 7 T
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: To examine whether longitudinal changes in frontoparietal (FP) - subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) joint temporal complexity differ between sgACC hemispheres in patients undergoing accelerated TMS (aTMS) and untreated healthy controls. Methods: Twenty-four patients with current depressive episodes and fifteen healthy controls underwent 7T resting-state fMRI at baseline and follow-up. Patients received aTMS localized to the left DLPFC using Beam-F3. The same bilateral FP time series was paired separately with left and right sgACC time series. Bivariate multiscale sample entropy (bMSE) across scale factors a1-a10 was summarized by trapezoidal integration as a complexity index (bMSE-CI). The primary test was the Group x Time x sgACC Hemisphere interaction in a mixed repeated-measures ANOVA. Scale-specific interactions and clinical Spearman correlations were evaluated with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Change scores were follow-up minus baseline. Results: The bMSE-CI Group x Time x Hemisphere interaction was significant (F(1,37) = 6.043, p = 0.0188, partial Eta squared = 0.140). Mean left/right bMSE-CI changes were -0.286/+0.124 in patients and +0.323/+0.112 in controls. Of ten scale-specific three-way interactions, only a2 survived FDR correction (q = 0.0435). No baseline or change-score bMSE-MADRS association survived the specified FDR corrections. A random-intercept-only mixed-model sensitivity analysis did not reach statistical significance for the three-way interaction (p = 0.0718). Conclusion: FP-sgACC joint temporal complexity showed hemisphere-dependent longitudinal differences between patients undergoing aTMS and healthy controls. These exploratory findings motivate further evaluation of bMSE as a candidate measure of longitudinal neural change in depression. Independent replication, more precise reliability estimates, and prospective validation of clinical relevance are needed.

item.title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

item.title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.

item.title: Middle Temporal Gyrus Neurite Microstructure and Scam Susceptibility in Older Adults Without Dementia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Financial exploitation is a prevalent public health concern among older adults, and emerging evidence links vulnerability to gray matter macrostructure and white matter microstructure, including within brain regions and networks implicated in early Alzheimer's disease. Although diffusion tensor imaging is sensitive to age-related variation in brain microstructure, its scalar metrics cannot distinguish among the tissue properties contributing to observed differences. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) models distinct tissue compartments, yielding estimates of neurite density, dendritic complexity, and extracellular free water. Methods: This study examined associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla imaging in 116 older adults without dementia. Neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and free-water fraction were quantified within seven a priori regions of interest linked to early Alzheimer's disease. Multivariate regressions evaluated associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics, adjusting for age, sex, education, and global cognition, with multiple comparison correction within each metric. For significant regions, post-hoc hierarchical regression models tested whether NODDI metrics explained variance beyond regional cortical thickness, total gray matter, and total intracranial volume. Results: Greater scam susceptibility was associated with higher NDI (β=0.30, pFDR=.025) and lower ODI (β=-0.28, pFDR=.044) in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG). No other regions survived correction. Additionally, MTG NDI and ODI explained variance beyond macrostructure measures. Conclusions: These findings identify NODDI metrics as novel microstructural correlates of scam susceptibility beyond macrostructure, supporting investigation of their relevance to financial vulnerability in older age.

item.title: Denoised gray matter BOLD-CSF coupling in aging and its association with markers of preclinical AD
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Global gray matter (gGM) blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal fluctuations are temporally coupled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflow. Reduced gGM BOLD-CSF coupling has been reported in aging and linked to Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related pathology. Our study aimed to investigate the effect of multi-echo denoising on age-related reductions in coupling and whether coupling is associated with cortical thickness across AD-vulnerable regions and crystallized–fluid ability (‘CF’) discrepancy, markers of preclinical AD. We analyzed an open-access behavioral/MRI dataset (n = 301) cognitively healthy younger and older adults (OpenNeuro ds003592). Coupling scores were calculated as correlations between gGM signal fluctuations and CSF inflow signals, before and after denoising. Linear mixed models tested the effects of age and denoising on coupling, while multiple regression models assessed associations between denoised coupling, cortical thickness, and CFdiscrepancy. Coupling was lower in older versus younger adults. Denoising significantly reduced coupling in younger adults but not in older adults. Both gGM and CSF signal amplitudes were lower in older adults. Denoised coupling was not significantly associated with cortical thickness or CFdiscrepancy, and cortical thickness was not associated with CFdiscrepancy after controlling for age. These findings support age-related differences in BOLD–CSF coupling, which itself may not be related to coarse markers of preclinical AD.

item.title: Central Motor Injury as Interlayer Decoupling: An Evolutionary Information Layering Framework for Neurorehabilitation
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Central motor injury is often framed as a loss of cortical command, leading rehabilitation to prioritize early cortical reactivation and active task practice. This framing captures an important part of motor impairment but leaves a second problem under-specified: how injury disrupts communication among mechanical, spinal-peripheral, and supraspinal coordination layers. The Evolutionary Information Layering (EIL) framework proposes that biological coordination develops through the retention, specialization, and integration of ancestral regulatory systems rather than through their replacement. Applying EIL to neurorehabilitation, this article conceptualizes severe central motor injury as interlayer decoupling, defined here as a loss of phase-, context-, and task-appropriate conditional influence among functional layers. Three interacting disturbances are proposed: reduced reliability of descending commands, maladaptive gain from residual descending activity, and preserved but insufficiently engaged lower-layer mechanical and spinal coordination. Rehabilitation can therefore be organized as layer reweighting rather than as competition between cortical and spinal mechanisms. The therapeutic sequence is to titrate premature higher-layer demand, re-engage structured lower-layer information, and progressively reintegrate higher-level predictive control. The framework generates testable predictions concerning phase-dependent spinal modulation, proximal coordination, and task-specific cortical engagement. It also provides a theoretical basis for lower-layer-informed rehabilitation protocols without claiming that spinal circuits replace cortical function. Because most indirect evidence comes from stroke and human locomotor or spinal cord studies, application to traumatic brain injury and other central nervous system disorders should remain diagnosis-dependent.

item.title: Age-related processes impacting cognitive processing speed across an older adult cohort: A drift diffusion model analysis.
item.description:
PloS one
The time we take to perform a cognitive task increases with age, which is a principal contributor to cognitive aging. The drift diffusion model is widely applied to decompose processes that may contribute to age-related slowing, with the drift rate parameter reflecting the rate of information accumulation until a decision is made. This age-related slowing is hypothesized to relate to changes in cerebral white matter microstructure. Our aim in this preregistered study (https://osf.io/yhn4m) was to evaluate the cross-sectional age-related differences in processes underlying age-related slowing across an older adult cohort and explore the role of white matter change in such age-related slowing. We found age to be associated with drift rate in an emotion recognition and a memory task but not in a delay discounting task; in an exploratory analysis, an indirect association involving global fractional anisotropy was observed for the emotion recognition task, although this did not survive multiple-comparison correction. Our results suggest age-related differences in information processing across cognitive contexts, although formal comparisons between tasks were not conducted. A fuller understanding of the mechanisms of cognitive slowing with age will help tailor intervention strategies and could inform environmental modifications promoting older adults' functional independence and quality of life.

item.title: Children with developmental language disorder show selective impairments in low-frequency neural tracking of speech.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Neural tracking of slow temporal modulations in speech supports extraction of the prosodic and syllabic structure thought to be critical for language acquisition by Temporal Sampling (TS) theory, yet whether these automatic cortical tracking mechanisms are altered in children with developmental language disorder (DLD) remains unclear. We recorded MEG while children with and without DLD listened to a story, and quantified source-level lagged speech-brain coherence and frequency-specific cortical functional connectivity across bilateral cortical regions. As expected a priori by TS theory, children with DLD showed significantly reduced coherence in the 0.9-2.5 Hz range associated with prosodic information in the story, spanning bilateral auditory and speech-related cortex. The strongest regional group differences were in left supramarginal gyrus (p < 0.001) and right inferior frontal gyrus (p = 0.001). In the 2.5-5 Hz range, linked to syllabic-rate modulations in the story, children with DLD showed reduced coherence in right temporal regions (all p < 0.02). Stronger low-frequency speech-brain coherence was associated with better language performance, indicating that individual differences in cortical speech tracking were behaviourally meaningful. No reliable differences were observed at higher modulation rates (5-9 Hz or 12-40 Hz). Exploratory functional connectivity analyses did not reveal network-level group differences that were robust across ROI time-series extraction methods. These findings indicate that atypical low-frequency neural tracking of speech is functionally relevant to language outcomes in DLD.

item.title: Olfactory network variability is associated with odor identification and cognitive performance in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundOdor identification impairment is an early marker of Alzheimer's disease pathology and predicts dementia conversion in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). However, the pathophysiological role of dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) variability within olfactory networks remains unclear.ObjectiveTo characterize seed-based dFC variability across olfactory pathways in MCI with odor identification impairment (MCI-OII) and examine its associations with olfactory and cognitive performance.MethodsNinety-seven patients with MCI were recruited and subdivided into MCI-OII and those without odor identification impairment (MCI-NOII), along with 97 age-matched healthy controls (HC). All participants underwent neuropsychological assessment, olfactory testing, and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Seed-based dFC variability was computed using a sliding window approach. Correlation and exploratory mediation analyses examined associations among abnormal dFC, odor identification, and cognition.ResultsCompared to MCI-NOII and HC, MCI-OII exhibited increased dFC variability between the left piriform cortex/right insula and right caudate nucleus, and between the left insula and left middle frontal gyrus. For the connection between the left insula and left cerebellar lobule VI, dFC variability showed a graded pattern from MCI-OII to HC to MCI-NOII. Increased caudate-centered dFC variability was associated with poorer odor identification, memory, and executive performance. Furthermore, exploratory mediation analyses suggested indirect associations involving odor identification, caudate-centered dFC variability, and memory or executive function.ConclusionsMCI-OII is characterized by increased olfactory-network dFC variability, particularly in caudate-centered pathways. These findings suggest that dFC variability may serve as a candidate network-level marker of concurrent olfactory impairment and cognitive dysfunction in MCI.

item.title: Developmental Aspects of Language Mapping with Stereoelectroencephalography.
item.description:
Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
This review examines developmental perspectives on the use of stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) for delineating language areas and networks in pediatric patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, both as a clinical tool for presurgical evaluation and as a modality for gaining neuroscientific insights into speech and language development. Language development is a dynamic process that begins before birth and continues into adulthood, shaped by the maturation of brain networks. SEEG allows high-resolution study of these networks, providing a unique perspective on the organization of language systems. This review traces language acquisition from early infancy through adolescence and adulthood, highlighting the pivotal role of neural oscillations. We then summarize classical and contemporary neural models of language organization, highlighting the distributed and hierarchical networks, and emphasize the high spatial and temporal resolution of SEEG for presurgical planning that enables clinicians to optimize neurosurgical interventions while preserving essential language areas and the tracts connecting them. Our review also addresses the human brain's remarkable plasticity and capacity for reorganization, which are especially pronounced in children and vital for adaptation to and recovery from neurologic injury or surgery. We focus specifically on developmental reorganization in pediatric patients with drug-resistant epilepsy and its implications for language mapping with SEEG. The review concludes with recommendations for designing language-mapping batteries tailored to the unique needs of pediatric patients.

item.title: The aging human brain exhibits reduced hemodynamic and cerebrospinal fluid flow waves during sleep.
item.description:
Nature aging
Aging reduces the quality and quantity of sleep, and sleep disruption is predictive of neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. Sleep loss could affect brain health through disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation, which is important for brain homeostasis. In young adults, large CSF flow waves appear during non-rapid eye movement sleep; however, whether sleep-dependent brain fluid physiology changes in aging is not known. Here we imaged large-scale CSF flow and hemodynamics in young (18-39 years) and older (60-84 years) adults during nighttime sleep. Sleep-dependent CSF flow was reduced in older adults, and was linked to reduced EEG slow wave power, decreased global hemodynamic oscillations and gray matter atrophy. Using sensory and vasoactive stimuli to drive CSF flow, we found that both neural and cerebrovascular changes contributed to this disruption. These results demonstrate reduced CSF flow during sleep in human aging, before disease onset, and identify parallel neural and hemodynamic mechanisms contributing to this decline.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: The neuroscience of delirium: a perfect storm for acute brain dysfunction.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Delirium is a frequent and distressing neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by acute disturbances of attention, awareness and cognition. Delirium emerges in response to diverse medical insults, particularly in hospitalized patients. Despite its high prevalence and association with accelerated cognitive decline, dementia and mortality, the neurobiology of delirium remains incompletely understood, and there are no treatments for delirium. Evidence from electrophysiology, neuroimaging, biomarkers and emerging animal models has begun to clarify the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying delirium. Delirium can be conceptualized as the interaction of acute systemic or cerebral stressors with pre-existing vulnerabilities, creating a 'perfect storm' for brain dysfunction. Generalized electroencephalographic slowing and network disintegration are convergent signatures across diverse types of delirium. Disruptions in neuromodulatory systems, energy metabolism and neuroimmune signalling may underlie impairment of large-scale brain function. The mechanisms that drive acute delirium may also contribute to subsequent brain injury and long-term decline, compounding its broad personal and societal impact.

item.title: Mesoscale connectivity of substructures within the human amygdaloid complex.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The amygdala operates as an integrative network hub, participating in emotional, cognitive, and distributed neural circuit functions. Though once thought of as a single anatomical entity, the amygdala is increasingly being recognized as a complex network of functionally and anatomically distinct nuclei and substructures. Mesoscale diffusion MR images (250 μm isotropic acquisition, upsampled to 125 μm) of the post-mortem human temporal lobe were acquired to allow the identification of the structural components of the amygdaloid complex, which includes the amygdala, as well as the surrounding transitional areas. Amygdala nuclei, including their 13 subnuclei and related substructures were defined, delineated and segmented to generate a unique 3-dimensional visualization of the amygdaloid complex in its anatomical context. Volumetric analyses and scalar indices revealed its morphological and microstructural composition, whereas tractography exposed the intra-amygdala connectome. Both canonical and non-canonical pathways were identified and quantified for a more in-depth network analysis. A virtual dissection of pathways involving the lateral nucleus, which is the largest nucleus (33% of the amygdala), for instance, showed numerous extra-amygdala pathways, as well as intra-amygdala pathways, consistent with its well-established role as the primary input site to the amygdala. A majority of connections are localized in the dorsal lateral subnucleus, which can be conceived of as the dominant gateway for afferent integration. In contrast, the central nucleus, emerged as the primary output hub from the amygdala. This intra-amygdala connectome framework establishes a structural roadmap that advances a mechanistic understanding and informs future network-based therapeutic strategies for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Altered individual-level morphological similarity brain networks in late-life subthreshold depression: Preserved global topology with selective nodal and sub-network disruptions.
item.description:
International psychogeriatrics
Subthreshold depression (StD) is prevalent in older adults and increases the risk of major depressive disorder, but its large-scale brain-network organization remains poorly understood. Individual-level morphological similarity networks estimate interregional structural covariance separately for each participant. 110 older women (56 StD, 54 comparison participants) underwent T1-weighted MRI. Individual networks were constructed using Jensen-Shannon divergence-based similarity (JSDs) between gray matter volume distributions across 116 AAL regions. Graph metrics were assessed across sparsity 0.05-0.40 with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) control, and the network-based statistic identified altered sub-networks (5000 permutations, FWE-corrected). Reproducibility was tested with an alternative Kullback-Leibler metric (KLDs) and 4-mm smoothing. Both groups showed preserved small-world global topology. Participants with StD had increased left hippocampal degree centrality (p = 0.0013), reduced nodal efficiency in the right inferior occipital (p = 0.0046) and right postcentral gyri (p = 0.0085), and a 50-node, 73-edge hypoconnectivity sub-network (pFWE = 0.0408); none of these regional findings survived FDR correction. Right inferior occipital efficiency was inversely associated with reminiscence and rumination, and right postcentral efficiency positively with cognition and extraversion. The hippocampal finding was reproduced using KLDs (p = 0.0012) and 4-mm smoothing (p = 0.0049). In 74 patients with major depressive disorder, global topology was likewise preserved but without corresponding nodal alterations. Late-life StD shows preserved global topology with focal nodal and sub-network disruptions. Hippocampal hyper-connectivity may reflect compensatory reorganization, whereas occipitotemporal and somatosensory hypoconnectivity is associated with reminiscence, rumination and cognitive function. Individual-level networks may provide a sensitive framework for characterising subclinical network alterations, pending confirmation in larger samples.

item.title: Hemisphere-specific neuroplasticity after basal ganglia stroke: divergent patterns of brain reorganization revealed by fALFF and ReHo.
item.description:
Brain research
Lesion laterality modulates post-stroke neuroplasticity following basal ganglia infarction, but hemisphere-specific reorganization patterns of motor circuits remain unclear. To investigate lateralized changes in spontaneous brain activity and local synchronization in patients with left versus right basal ganglia infarction using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), and to explore their associations with motor recovery. Resting-state fMRI-derived fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were analyzed in 31 patients with left basal ganglia infarction (LBGIS), 33 patients with right basal ganglia infarction (RBGIS), and 33 healthy controls. TFCE-FWE corrected two-sample t-tests and covariate-adjusted partial correlations were used to compare brain activity and link functional alterations to Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) motor scores. LBGIS displayed hypoactivity in ipsilesional motor cortices alongside hyperactivation of contralesional cerebellum and prefrontal areas; ipsilesional sensorimotor ReHo positively correlated with FMA, whereas contralesional cerebellar fALFF negatively correlated with FMA. RBGIS showed reduced ipsilesional frontoparietal activity and isolated hyper-synchronization within the ipsilesional frontoparietal motor network without cerebellar recruitment, with elevated ReHo in ipsilesional precentral gyrus/SMA negatively associated with FMA. Direct group comparisons validated stronger bilateral motor-planning and contralesional cerebellar signals in LBGIS, and higher right visual-spatial fALFF in RBGIS. Left and right basal ganglia infarctions elicit divergent hemispheric neuroplastic modifications in motor networks. These lateralized functional signatures could serve as imaging biomarkers for lesion-side-customized motor rehabilitation.

item.title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

item.title: The role of semantically related co-speech gestures in English-to-Chinese consecutive interpreting: a behavioral and ERP study.
item.description:
Acta psychologica
Co-speech gestures are an important source of visual-semantic information in communication, yet how the semantic relatedness of speech and gesture influences both comprehension and production during consecutive interpreting (CI) remains insufficiently understood. To this end, the present study combined behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) measure to examine how semantically related and semantically unrelated co-speech gestures affect source-language comprehension and target-language production in English-to-Chinese CI through a cue-recall task and oral translation. The comprehension-related results showed that gesture condition did not significantly affect cue-recall accuracy, but semantically related gestures were associated with faster responses than semantically unrelated gestures. ERP results during real-time comprehension further showed that semantically related gestures elicited less negative N400 amplitudes, which were distributed along the anterior-posterior scalp axis and maximal over parietal sites. The production-related results showed translation scores were also higher in the semantically related gesture condition. These effects remained stable after verbal working memory was included as a covariate. Overall, the findings provide initial behavioral and neurocognitive evidence that co-speech gestures are integrated with speech during CI, and that reduced semantic relatedness between speech and gesture increases online semantic processing demands with downstream consequences for target-language production. The study advances a multimodal account of consecutive interpreting by showing that visually available co-speech gestures shape both source-language comprehension and subsequent target-language production.

item.title: Whole-brain white matter fractional anisotropy across baseball expertise levels: a TBSS study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
While sports-related sensorimotor experience has been associated with differences in brain structure and function, evidence regarding white matter (WM) microstructural differences in high-speed open-skilled sports remains limited. Prior studies have often been constrained by small sample sizes or analyses restricted to selected tracts. To address these limitations, this study employed voxel-wise tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to examine whole-brain fractional anisotropy (FA) in 142 participants: 50 highly skilled baseball (SB) players, 45 intermediate baseball (IB) players, and 47 non-player (NP) controls. TBSS revealed that the SB group exhibited significantly higher FA than the IB and/or NP groups across multiple projection and cerebellar pathways, including the pontine crossing tract, corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, superior cerebellar peduncle, and cerebral peduncle, as well as association pathways (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus and sagittal stratum), commissural pathways (corpus callosum and tapetum), and the fornix (crus)/stria terminalis. Follow-up ROI analyses showed significant group effects in seven of 16 selected tracts, including the pontine crossing tract, body of the corpus callosum, left superior corona radiata, bilateral posterior corona radiata, and bilateral tapetum. Across these tracts, the SB group consistently demonstrated higher FA than the IB and/or NP groups. Together, these results indicate that FA differences across expertise levels were primarily characterized by higher values in skilled players rather than a uniform increase across the three groups. These findings suggest that high-level baseball expertise is associated with spatially distributed WM microstructural differences across multiple neural systems implicated in sensorimotor, visuospatial, cerebellar, and interhemispheric processing.

item.title: Microstructural alterations of human medial temporal lobe in dementia: volumetric and DTI findings correlate with cell number and neuropathology.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Volumetric and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) alterations in medial temporal lobe (MTL) regions are consistently reported in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, their biological basis remains poorly understood. We combined Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) metrics with cellular quantification and neuropathological burden assessment to investigate microstructural substrates underlying MTL imaging alterations in human donors with known cognitive and neuropathological status. Absolute cell numbers were quantified in a cohort of 54 brain donors using the isotropic fractionator, and postmortem MRI was performed on a subset of 18 fixed brain hemispheres. To assess microstructural brain alterations associated with disease progression, in vivo volumetric and DTI metrics were analyzed in 39 cognitively unimpaired controls (CU), 31 individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 14 patients with clinical AD dementia. In the postmortem cohort, MTL diffusivity metrics showed moderate negative correlations with total cell numbers. Mean, axial, and radial diffusivity positively correlated with Braak stage, whereas fractional anisotropy (FA) correlated negatively with CERAD score, linking diffusion alterations to AD-related pathology. In vivo MTL analyses revealed increased mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, and reduced FA in AD patients compared with both CU and MCI individuals. The MCI group exhibited intermediate alterations in diffusivity. Differences between in vivo and postmortem diffusion values were consistent with tissue fixation, temperature, and variations in acquisition protocols. Our findings suggest that diffusion MRI alterations in the MTL are associated with reduced cellularity and neuropathological burden, supporting the biological relevance of DTI metrics as markers of microstructural degeneration in AD.

item.title: MRI Microscopic Fractional Anisotropy Differences in Genetic Frontotemporal Degeneration.
item.description:
Journal of magnetic resonance imaging : JMRI
Background In genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), cortical and subcortical brain volume differences have been detected using volumetric MRI decades before symptoms appear. Microscopic fractional anisotropy (μFA) is a diffusion MRI metric that is sensitive to diffusion anisotropy regardless of relative fiber orientations within a voxel and is more accurate than conventional DTI metrics for detecting age-related microstructural changes in healthy individuals and differences in some neurological diseases. Purpose To compare μFA, mean diffusivity (MD), and volume between genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) variant carriers and non-carriers in the insula, frontal pole, and medial orbitofrontal cortex. Study type Cross-sectional cohort study. Population Carriers of FTD variants in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT (n = 12; age = 56.7 ± 8.12 years; 50% female) and familial non-variant carriers (n = 8; age = 59.5 ± 10.3 years; 62.5% female). Field strength/sequence 3T; Magnetization prepared rapid acquisition with gradient echoes (MPRAGE) sequence (anatomical imaging) and a diffusion echo-planar imaging sequence with modified diffusion gradients for spherical tensor encoding (μFA measurement). Assessment MPRAGE images underwent cortical and subcortical segmentation to obtain regions of interest. MD and μFA maps were derived from diffusion MRI data. μFA, MD, and volumes were compared between FTD variant carriers (n = 5 symptomatic, and n = 7 asymptomatic) and familial non-carriers. Statistical tests Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent confidence intervals were computed to analyze between-group differences in outcomes while controlling for age (alpha = 0.05). Results FTD variant carriers exhibited significantly lower insula μFA than non-carriers (η2 p = 0.22). Post hoc contrasts showed significantly reduced insula μFA in symptomatic carriers compared to non-carriers (d = 1.57). Mean μFA in asymptomatic carriers (mean ± standard error (SE): 0.454 ± 0.010) was not significantly different to that in non-carriers (mean ± SE: 0.471 ± 0.009, p = 0.465), nor in symptomatic carriers (mean ± SE: 0.430 ± 0.012, p = 0.290). Data conclusion μFA is reduced in the insula, a region vulnerable to early atrophy in FTD, reflecting microstructural changes in genetic FTD with greater effect sizes than MD and volume. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy Stage 2.

item.title: Sentence-level neural dynamics in speech motor cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Prior recordings from speech motor cortex have revealed phonemic, syllabic, articulatory and speech-sequence representations, while more recent studies indicate that activity may also reflect higher-order features of speech production. However, whether speech motor cortex is sensitive to the linguistic organization of sentences remains unclear. Here we show that single-unit activity in speech motor cortex contains information about sentence-level linguistic structure. In three BrainGate2 participants with implanted microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, we recorded neural activity during an instructed-delay speech task comprising English sentences, word lists, syntactically structured nonword sentences and nonword lists. Neural activity in areas 6v and 55b contained speech- and language-related components, with stronger stimulus-condition effects in 55b, and stimulus condition was decodable in all three participants. In two larger datasets, semantic categories of English sentences were decodable from neural activity. These findings demonstrate that speech motor cortex encodes information about linguistic structure and semantic content at the level of sentences.

item.title: The extended default mode network dysconnectivity in schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The default mode network (DMN) extends beyond cortex into subcortical structures, yet how this extended DMN (eDMN) is causally reorganized in schizophrenia (SZ) remains unclear. Here, resting-state fMRI from 74 healthy controls (HC) and 66 SZ patients was analyzed. Subject-specific eDMNs were identified using spatially-constrained independent component analysis, and effective connectivity among 13 regions was estimated with spectral dynamic causal modeling, with group effects assessed using parametric empirical Bayes. Causal centrality—a dynamics-sensitive and causality-based measure of nodal importance—was computed per region, compared between groups, and correlated with MATRICS cognitive scores in patients. Causal centrality rankings were highly similar across groups (ρ = 0.87), with both favoring subcortical over cortical regions. Group differences were regionally specific: temporal cortex was more causally central in patients, whereas posterior parietal cortex was more causally central in controls. Most connection-level SZ-HC differences originated from ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, prefrontal cortex, basal forebrain, temporal cortex, and thalamus. In patients, temporal causal centrality correlated negatively with reasoning/problem-solving, and ventrolateral prefrontal causal centrality with processing speed and composite cognition. The eDMN's core causal architecture is preserved in schizophrenia, but temporal influence is enhanced and parietal influence attenuated—alterations that are behaviorally meaningful and consistent with pathological reorganization.

item.title: DECODE: DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States: Separating Structure-Coupled and Structure-Decoupled Functional Organization in Alzheimers Disease
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain functional activity emerges within an underlying structural scaffold. While structural network connectivity provides a relatively stable anatomical backbone for large-scale communication, functional interactions are high-dimensional and temporally dynamic, forming recurrent patterns that can be represented in a latent space of transient functional states. Yet, how these transient functional states are organized and the extent to which they remain constrained by structural network connectivity or become relatively decoupled from structural organization over time remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce DECODE (DEcomposition of COupled and DEcoupled Brain States), a data-driven latent-space framework that uses independent component analysis (ICA) and multimodal data to decompose resting-state dynamic functional network connectivity into a lower-dimensional representation of transient functional states. These states capture temporally varying structure-coupled and structure-decoupled patterns using diffusion MRI-derived structural network connectivity priors. Structure-coupled states reflect functional configurations more strongly anchored to major structural motifs, whereas structure-decoupled states represent configurations less constrained by the identified structural organization, while potentially remaining within structurally defined dynamical bounds. DECODE identifies reproducible structure-coupled and structure-decoupled states, with mean squared error reconstruction of dynamic information < 0.1 and adjusted R-squared = 0.4. Applied to Alzheimers disease (AD), DECODE revealed stronger group differences (FDR-corrected p-value 0.05) in both connectivity organization and temporal dynamics for decoupled states. These findings suggest that functional states less constrained by identified structural organization may be more vulnerable to AD-related disruption, whereas structure-coupled states may be relatively preserved. More broadly, DECODE provides a reproducible and generalizable framework for quantifying how functional dynamics are shaped by, or diverge from, structural organization by incorporating a latent representation of the structural connectome as an informative prior. Our findings established structural and functional alignment variation by distinguishing dynamic functional patterns closely coupled with structure from those that deviate from it.

item.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging Phenotypes in Cognitively Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in cognitively healthy older adults remains unclear. Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling. Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 14 were cohort studies (nine observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2.5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and smaller medial temporal and hippocampal volumes; greenspace was associated with more favourable brain structure in several mostly cross-sectional studies, though findings were not uniform. Thirteen studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low though not uniform risk of bias; outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 27 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.Interpretation: This review synthesises emerging observational evidence that air pollution is associated with differences in brain structure in cognitively healthy ageing. Because the included evidence is predominantly cross-sectional, these associations are hypothesis generating; if confirmed in longitudinal studies, this modifiable exposure could serve as a potential target for policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

item.title: From the app to the lexicon: Neurocognitive markers of word integration in a second language
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition. However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes. In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration. Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic decision task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs. Critically, L2 targets were classified as remote (learned earlier during the five-week training and not practiced in the final stage) or recent (learned in the final training stage and tested approximately 10 days later), allowing us to assess consolidation-related differences. Behaviorally, participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words, and accuracy for related items was higher for remotely than recently learned items, consistent with consolidation-related strengthening. Electrophysiologically, robust N400 priming effects emerged for remotely learned words—whereas no facilitation was observed for recent words. This graded pattern suggests that only words with extended consolidation time exhibited neural markers of lexical–semantic integration. Together, these findings demonstrate that combining real-world digital learning with controlled neural testing can reveal how naturalistic language experience shapes the neurocognitive dynamics of word learning and consolidation.

item.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) are associated with reading ability, yet evidence on whether SL is impaired in Developmental Dyslexia (DD) is inconsistent. Furthermore, DD is associated with impairments in Rhythmic Ability (RA) and Working Memory (WM). This study examined SL in adults with self-reported diagnoses of DD compared to Typical Readers (TR), and explored whether individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary related to individual SL ability in speech segmentation.A total of 143 participants (N_DD = 25, N_TR = 118) were exposed to an artificial language of trisyllabic nonsense-words while neural entrainment to the words assessed SL via electroencephalography (EEG), followed by behavioral SL outcome measures. Aiming to assess individual differences, we linked the neural measure of SL to a battery of tests measuring musicality, RA, WM, and vocabulary size. Results indicated neural evidence for SL in both groups, with similar neural entrainment to the structure during exposure. Behavioral performance in the DD group on SL seemed below TR, though Bayesian analyses rendered this inconclusive. The DD group obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM and vocabulary size, which was primarily driven by the latter two. Comparison of relations between neural SL and these tasks indicated no group differences therein. Exploratively combining the groups into one population resulted in anecdotal Bayesian evidence that individual differences in SL related to WM and RA measured by sensorimotor synchronization, which was rendered inconclusive in sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons.

item.title: Allometric scaling of resting-state EEG network topography across childhood and adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Brain network topography undergoes complex reorganization throughout childhood and adolescence. Quantifying the functional form of this maturation remains a key challenge. Here, we applied developmental allometry to sensor-level resting-state EEG networks from 1,957 participants aged 5–21 years (Healthy Brain Network). We fitted power laws of age to four graph-theoretic indices (small-worldness, global and local efficiency, modularity) across five frequency bands. Nineteen of the 20 band-by-index exponents were negative. Low-frequency (delta and theta) small-worldness showed the steepest declines (alpha = -0.878 and − 0.868), indicating a near-halving of the metric with each doubling of age. Lobe-resolved analyses revealed a pan-lobar but non-uniform decline, with posterior regions showing steeper age-related changes than frontal regions in specific bands. While raw-space cross-validation did not uniquely favor the power law over linear models, its scale-free exponent provides a unified parameter to compare developmental rates across spatial and spectral scales. Individual deviations from this topology did not track dimensional psychopathology. These exponents provide a quantitative reference for EEG network topography maturation and highlight the necessity of frequency- and region-specific modeling.

item.title: A realistic model of resting-state BOLD spectra in white matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state BOLD signals in white matter show a spectral elevation near 0.06 Hz on an exponentially decaying background, and white-matter hemodynamic response functions (HRFs) have a prominent initial dip. We model the resting signal as shot noise: randomly timed neural events are filtered by the HRF, so that the spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the squared HRF gain, plus instrumental noise. The initial dip and post-stimulus undershoot remove low-frequency power, making the white-matter HRF a band-pass filter with maximum gain near 0.05 Hz. One set of physiological parameters fits both a measured white-matter HRF (R² = 0.993) and the group-mean white-matter spectrum (R² = 0.987), with a resting transit time of about 4 s and a metabolic response weighted about twice as heavily as in gray matter. Deepening the dip raises the filter gain and moves its maximum toward 0.06 Hz, linking the dip to the spectral feature. A narrower line in individual spectra is reproduced either by an underdamped HRF that matches the measured response over its first 20 s or by a rhythmic input near 0.06 Hz. The model identifies which HRF properties could explain the decline of the peak with age.

item.title: Opposite Modulations of Thalamo-Cingulate and Fronto-IFOF Gray-White Matter Circuits Underlie Symptomatic and Cognitive Gains with Magnetic Seizure Therapy in Schizophrenia
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) has shown promise for treating schizophrenia, but the functional brain changes associated with its clinical and cognitive outcomes remain unclear. We investigated gray matter–white matter (GM–WM) functional connectivity and its associations with symptom and cognitive changes following MST. Fifty-three patients with schizophrenia and 40 demographically matched healthy controls underwent baseline resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging; 33 patients with usable pretreatment and post-treatment imaging data were included in longitudinal analyses. Functional connectivity was compared between groups and across treatment time points, and connectivity changes were examined in relation to clinical and cognitive changes. Following MST, patients showed reductions in psychotic symptoms and improvements in the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery composite score and processing speed. Treatment-related connectivity changes predominantly involved GM–WM connections. Decreased connectivity within a thalamus–corona radiata–cingulate circuit was associated with symptom improvement, whereas increased connectivity involving the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and frontal regions was associated with cognitive improvement. Exploratory atlas-based analyses identified spatial associations between functional connectivity patterns and normative histaminergic and serotonergic receptor distributions, including 5-HT4 receptor maps. These findings suggest that symptom and cognitive improvements following MST are associated with changes in GM–WM functional connectivity. The receptor mapping results provide an exploratory neurochemical context for these associations, rather than evidence of treatment-induced changes in neurotransmitter levels or receptor availability.

item.title: Cross-Condition Transfer Learning for EEG-Based Inner Speech Classification: A Controlled Evaluation of Neural Networks and Temporal Segmentation
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Transferring a decoder trained on overt (pronounced) speech to inner speech has been proposed to offset scarce inner-speech EEG. This was re-examined on the “Thinking out loud” dataset (ds003626, 10 participants, four words), with no test trial in training or selection. EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, CSP+LDA and a Riemannian tangent-space pipeline were compared on bidirectional transfer, combined training, overt pre-training with fine-tuning on 25–100% inner-speech subsets, maximum-mean-discrepancy alignment and four trial windows. Shuffled-label controls and an exploratory, post hoc test family were used. Cross-participant, held-out-session, channel, band, external-electrode and second-dataset (ds006104) arms were reference checks. Within participant, overt speech was decodable in the action interval (0.34–0.43, chance 0.250). It survived a held-out session, peaked in 30–100 Hz and did not cross participants. Two lip electrodes alone decoded the pronounced word at 0.67–0.83. Regressing the external electrodes out of the scalp reduced three decoders’ overt accuracy to 0.28–0.40, leaving a residual of undetermined origin. Inner-speech accuracy was not distinguishable from chance. No transfer method, fine-tuned or not, improved reliably on its controls. Effects below about 2–6 percentage points were likely missed. These findings suggest that articulation-related features learned from overt speech may not provide sufficiently transferable information for inner-speech decoding under the present conditions.

item.title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions.Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.

item.title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of 'alien identity' and two classes of 'alien size.' Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

item.title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

item.title: Dynamic Brain Network Transitions and Sensorimotor Performance Across the Adult Lifespan.
item.description:
Seminars in ultrasound, CT, and MR
Background & objectives Healthy adult aging is accompanied by subtle variations in fine sensorimotor control and cognitive flexibility. Traditional static neuroimaging approaches often overlook short-term temporal dynamics. This study investigated cross-sectional associations between temporal brain state transitions and sensorimotor performance-specifically force matching and motor learning adaptation-across the adult lifespan. Methods Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and behavioral data from 218 healthy adults (aged 18-88 years; 99 females, 119 males) were analyzed across three age groups: young (18-35 years; n = 45; 25 females, 20 males), middle-aged (>35-60 years; n = 88; 37 females, 51 males), and older adults (>60 years; n = 85; 37 females, 48 males).Sex distribution did not differ significantly across age groups (p = 0.302). Time varying functional connectivity was modeled to extract Fractional Occupancy (FO), Mean Dwell Time (MDT), and global Switching Rate (SR) across six recurrent brain states. Behavioral metrics included finger force overcompensation (force matching) and spatial trajectory error during late-exposure motor learning. Results Advancing age was significantly associated with higher trajectory error during motor learning (p < 0.001) and greater force overcompensation (p ≤ 0.001). Post-hoc comparisons revealed non-linear cross-sectional differences, with older adults exhibiting higher error margins than young and middle-aged groups. Global switching rate (SR) demonstrated a statistically significant inverse association with motor learning error (β = -0.122 to -0.280, p < 0.03), indicating that higher dynamic network flexibility is associated with lower motor adaptation error. Furthermore, age was negatively correlated with switching rate (β = -0.166, p = 0.023). In the Executive Control Network (State 3), females exhibited significantly higher FO (p = 0.003) and adjusted MDT (p = 0.007) compared to males. Additionally, older males showed a nominal positive association with Task-Positive Network (State 5) dwell time (ρ = 0.204, p = 0.026). Conclusion These findings suggest an age-associated pattern of "dynamic rigidity," characterized by a reduced propensity for global brain state switching within cross-sectional observations. Fluid state transition capacity-rather than isolated state occupancy-offers significant explanatory relevance for sensorimotor adaptation across the adult lifespan.

item.title: High cortical lesion burden moderates the association between brain networks and processing speed in older adults with multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Cortical lesions (CL) are common in older adults with multiple sclerosis (OAMS), but their influence on the relationship between resting-state network strength (RSNS) and cognitive function in OAMS remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether CL moderates associations between RSNS and processing speed in OAMS. 82 OAMS participants (mean age: 64.4 ± 4.1 years; males/females: 26/56) were scanned in a 3T scanner. Identification of CL on double inversion-recovery (DIR) MRI images in this study was performed using established consensus recommendations. We estimated functional brain networks using a data-driven procedure to extract seven intrinsic resting-state networks. The Symbol-Digit-Modalities Test (SDMT), an established test of processing speed and working memory, served as the cognitive outcome measure. Multiple linear regressions, adjusted for sociodemographic covariates, examined the relationship between RSNS and SDMT performance with CL (three levels: no CL, 1-2 CL, and ≥ 3 CL) as a moderator. Significant CL-by-network interactions in models adjusted for sociodemographic covariates and white matter lesion load indicated that high-burden CL vs. no CL moderated the association between RSNS and SDMT in the auditory network (AUD) (p = 0.030), dorsal attention network (DAN) (p = 0.033), left frontoparietal network (LFPN) (p = 0.030), and posterior DMN (pDMN) (p = 0.030). Conditional effects showed that high-burden CLs attenuated positive associations between specific brain networks and SDMT performance. These findings suggest that higher CL burden restricts the functional brain support for processing speed and working memory performance in OAMS.

item.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.
